question: What defines a unit test?
options: It exercises one small unit of behaviour in isolation from its dependencies
It runs the whole application end to end
It is any test written before the code
It is a test that touches the database
explanation: Isolation is what makes a unit test fast and precise: when it fails, only one thing can be wrong. Tests that cross real boundaries are integration tests.

question: What do the three As of the AAA pattern stand for?
options: Arrange, Act, Assert
Analyse, Apply, Approve
Assemble, Assert, Abort
Arrange, Assert, Amend
explanation: Set up the state, perform the one action under test, then check the outcome. Keeping the three phases visually separate makes the intent of a test obvious.

question: What distinguishes a mock from a stub?
options: A mock verifies that expected interactions happened; a stub just returns canned data
A stub verifies interactions; a mock only returns canned data
A mock is generated by a framework; a stub must be hand-written
They are the same thing under different names
explanation: Stubs exist to get the test past a dependency, so they answer queries. Mocks are part of the assertion, so they record and verify calls.

question: In xUnit, what does combining [Theory] with [InlineData] give you?
options: One parameterised test that runs once per data row
A test that is skipped unless data is supplied at runtime
A test that runs all rows and reports a single combined result
A performance benchmark across the supplied inputs
explanation: Each [InlineData] row becomes its own test case with its own pass or fail result, which is far more useful than looping inside a single [Fact].

question: What makes a test an integration test rather than a unit test?
options: It exercises several components together, often including a real dependency
It is written after the production code
It contains more than one assertion
It is run only in the build pipeline
explanation: Integration tests check that the wiring between parts is right, which is precisely what unit tests with mocked dependencies cannot tell you.

question: Which of these most often makes a test flaky?
options: Depending on shared mutable state, real clocks, or test execution order
Having a long and descriptive test name
Using a parameterised test instead of separate cases
Asserting on a value object rather than a primitive
explanation: Flakiness comes from hidden inputs the test does not control: leftover data, timing, ordering, or concurrency. Injecting a clock and isolating state removes most of it.

question: What does a code coverage percentage actually tell you?
options: How much of the code was executed by the tests, not whether it behaves correctly
The proportion of requirements that have been verified
How likely the code is to be bug-free
How many assertions the test suite contains
explanation: Coverage measures execution, not verification: a test with no assertions can still cover a line. It is useful for finding untested code, not for proving correctness.

question: What is the TDD cycle?
options: Write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor
Write the code, then the test, then refactor
Design, implement, document
Write all tests, write all code, then review
explanation: Red, green, refactor. Seeing the test fail first proves the test can detect the problem it claims to.

question: In xUnit, how do you get fresh setup for each test in a class?
options: Put it in the constructor; xUnit creates a new instance per test
Use a static initialiser, which xUnit resets between tests
Mark a method with [Setup]
Nothing is needed; xUnit rolls back all state automatically
explanation: xUnit constructs a new instance of the test class for every test, so constructor work is per-test setup and IDisposable.Dispose is teardown.

question: What is the purpose of a regression test?
options: To lock in a fixed bug so it cannot silently come back
To measure whether performance has degraded over time
To test the application under peak load
To confirm the code compiles on every supported platform
explanation: Writing a test that reproduces a bug before fixing it proves the fix works and keeps that behaviour asserted forever afterwards.

question: What is a test fixture?
options: The shared context or setup that a test runs against
An assertion comparing two objects for equality
A report listing which tests failed
A tool that generates random input data
explanation: The fixture is whatever has to exist before the test can act: objects under test, their collaborators, and any prepared data.

question: What is a fake, as distinct from a mock or a stub?
options: A working but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository
A double that records calls so they can be verified afterwards
A double that always throws an exception
A double generated at runtime through reflection
explanation: A fake really behaves like the thing it replaces, just more cheaply. Stubs only answer queries, and mocks exist to have their interactions asserted.

question: What does IClassFixture<T> give you in xUnit?
options: A brand new instance of T for every test
One instance of T shared by every test in the class
Automatic disposal after each assertion
Parallel execution of that class's tests
explanation: It exists for setup too expensive to repeat, such as starting a test host. Because the instance is shared, tests must not mutate it.

question: Why avoid asserting on implementation details?
options: Such assertions execute more slowly
The test then breaks during refactoring even when the behaviour is unchanged
Test frameworks cannot reach private members
It makes coverage figures inaccurate
explanation: A test coupled to how the code works stops being a safety net and becomes an obstacle, because every internal improvement produces a false failure.

question: Why does test-driven development insist you watch the test fail first?
options: It warms up the test runner's cache
The framework requires a failure before it will record a pass
A test that has never failed might not be asserting anything at all
It measures how long the fix takes to write
explanation: The red step verifies the test itself. A test with a broken setup, or asserting on the wrong thing, can pass for the wrong reason indefinitely.

question: What makes a good test name?
options: It states the scenario and the behaviour expected of it
It matches the name of the method under test exactly
It is short enough to fit in a single word
It records the ticket number and the author
explanation: The name is what you read in a failure report, so it should say what was expected without needing the body to be opened.

question: Why must tests not depend on the order they run in?
options: Runners may reorder or parallelise them, so order dependence causes intermittent failures
Ordered tests always execute more slowly
Coverage tools cannot process ordered tests
It is purely a stylistic preference with no practical effect
explanation: Order dependence means one test is quietly relying on another's leftover state, which also makes any single failure much harder to interpret.

question: What is a smoke test?
options: A quick check that the system starts and its main paths work
A test that deliberately crashes the application
A test measuring memory growth over time
A test that only runs after a release has shipped
explanation: Smoke tests are the shallow-but-broad first line of defence, meant to catch a fundamentally broken build before deeper suites spend time on it.

question: How does branch coverage differ from line coverage?
options: Branch coverage records whether each decision went both ways, not merely whether the line executed
Branch coverage counts only the lines inside if statements
Line coverage is always the lower of the two numbers
They are two names for the same measurement
explanation: A single test can execute an if statement's line while only ever taking the true path, so line coverage looks complete while half the logic is untested.

question: What is the risk of mocking too much?
options: The suite slows down as the number of mocks grows
Tests end up asserting how the code is wired rather than what it does, so any refactor breaks them
Mocks cannot be used with asynchronous code
The mocking framework runs out of proxy types
explanation: When every collaborator is a mock, the test restates the implementation. It will keep passing when the behaviour is wrong and fail when only the structure changes.

question: Why build test data through a builder or factory?
options: Each test can specify only the fields it cares about, keeping its intent visible
It is the only way to construct objects with private constructors
It guarantees the data would be valid in production
It makes the tests run in parallel automatically
explanation: Sensible defaults plus a single overridden field make the relevant input obvious, instead of burying it in twenty lines of irrelevant setup.

question: How should a test for an async method be written?
options: Return Task from the test method and await the call
Call .Result and assert on the value
Use a sleep to wait for completion
Declare the test as async void
explanation: Returning Task lets the runner await the test so failures and exceptions are observed. An async void test can report success while its assertions never ran.

question: Which inputs most deserve their own test?
options: Values comfortably inside the valid range
Boundaries and edges: empty, null, first, last, and one past the limit
Randomly generated values, regenerated on every run
Only values that have actually appeared in production
explanation: Bugs cluster at boundaries, because that is where off-by-one errors and unhandled empty cases live. The middle of the range rarely surprises anyone.

question: Why does a single flaky test matter so much?
options: It adds a measurable amount to the suite's runtime
It teaches the team to ignore a red build, which then hides real failures
It corrupts the coverage database
It only matters if it fails more than half the time
explanation: The damage is social rather than technical. Once re-running until green becomes the habit, the suite has stopped being a signal anyone trusts.

question: Why keep each test focused on a single behaviour?
options: A failure then points straight at one specific cause
Frameworks reject tests containing more than one assertion
It reduces the total number of tests required
Multiple assertions are not permitted in a single test
explanation: A focused test tells you what broke from its name alone. A test covering five behaviours only tells you that one of five things went wrong.
